\chapter{Having Gone, and In Order to Go}
\label{ch:sa-having-gone}
\hlchaptermodality{55}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put two actions in one Sanskrit clause — one finished before the other with -\sk{त्वा}, or one as the point of the other with -\sk{तुम्}.}

Complete SA-R55-non-finite and say both endings with one sentence apiece.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gatvā]{\sk{गत्वा} (gatvā) — having gone}

\label{lesson:SA-C55-gatva}



\begin{quote}
Say the teacher-and-boy sentence from the last chapter, and say where the inner clause stops. Then say \emph{gacchati} and what it means.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one action finished, the next beginning}]
Every verb you have used so far has been the main verb of its sentence. Sanskrit has a form that is deliberately \textbf{not} the main verb: it names an action that finished before the main one started, and it never changes its ending.

Add \textbf{-\sk{त्वा}} to the root and you have it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{गम्}} $\to$ \textbf{\sk{गत्वा}} — \emph{having gone}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{पठ्}} $\to$ \textbf{\sk{पठित्वा}} — \emph{having read}
\end{quote}

Now chain two actions in one clause, with one subject:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{बालः} \sk{गृहं} \sk{गत्वा} \sk{पठति}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bālaḥ gṛhaṁ gatvā paṭhati}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{the boy, having gone home, reads}
\end{quote}

Three things make this form worth its own lesson:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{It carries no person, no number and no tense.} \emph{gatvā} is the same word whoever went and whenever. The main verb at the end of the sentence carries all of that for both actions.
  \item \textbf{Both actions belong to the same subject.} The boy goes and the boy reads. If the subjects differed, this form could not be used.
  \item \textbf{It orders the actions.} \emph{gatvā paṭhati} can only mean going first and reading second. English needs a word — \emph{after}, \emph{then} — to fix the order. Sanskrit fixes it with the ending.
\end{enumerate}

This form has no English counterpart at all. \emph{Having gone} is the nearest, and it is stiff in a way \textbf{\sk{गत्वा}} is not: in Sanskrit this is ordinary, everyday, and extremely common.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two actions in one clause, in the order they happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gatvā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ gṛhaṁ gatvā paṭhati}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{paṭhitvā}, and say which action it puts first
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{गत्वा}}, and name the ending that makes it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \textbf{-\sk{त्वा}} ending do to a root? (Makes an action that finished before the main one.) Say the boy-goes-home-and-reads sentence.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gantum]{\sk{गन्तुम्} (gantum) — to go}

\label{lesson:SA-C55-gantum}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\sk{गत्वा}} and what its ending does. Which of the two actions in \emph{gṛhaṁ gatvā paṭhati} happened first?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the form that names the action itself}]
\textbf{-\sk{त्वा}} put an action \emph{before} another one. \textbf{-\sk{तुम्}} does something different: it names the action without placing it in time at all.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{गम्}} $\to$ \textbf{\sk{गन्तुम्}} — \emph{to go}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{पठ्}} $\to$ \textbf{\sk{पठितुम्}} — \emph{to read}
\end{quote}

Used on its own it says why:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{बालः} \sk{पठितुम्} \sk{गच्छति}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bālaḥ paṭhitum gacchati}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{the boy goes in order to read}
\end{quote}

Set the pair side by side and the division of labour is clean:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{ending} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\sk{गत्वा}} & -\sk{त्वा} & an action finished before the main one \\
\textbf{\sk{गन्तुम्}} & -\sk{तुम्} & the action named, with no time of its own \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Now the part that is worth stopping for. Latin has a form called the \textbf{supine}, used after verbs of motion to say why you went — and it ends in \textbf{-tum}: \emph{īre dormītum}, \textquotedblleft{}to go to sleep\textquotedblright{}; \emph{spectātum venīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to come to watch\textquotedblright{}. That is the same ending, in the same job, inherited from the same ancestor. Not a borrowing and not a coincidence: Sanskrit \textbf{-\sk{तुम्}} and Latin \emph{-tum} are one suffix, split apart before either language existed.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both non-finite forms, and a reason to go somewhere.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gantum}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ paṭhitum gacchati}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{paṭhitvā gacchati} and \emph{paṭhitum gacchati}, and say what each one means
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{गन्तुम्}}, and name the Latin ending it matches
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending names the action itself, \textbf{-\sk{त्वा}} or \textbf{-\sk{तुम्}}? Say \textquotedblleft{}the boy goes in order to read\textquotedblright{}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-tvā · -tum]{-\sk{त्वा} · -\sk{तुम्} — the two endings, reviewed}

\label{lesson:SA-R55-non-finite}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\sk{गत्वा}} and \textbf{\sk{गन्तुम्}}, and say which one puts its action first.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both of these endings do the same large thing: they let a sentence hold \textbf{two actions with one finite verb}. Everything about person, number and tense is carried by the verb at the end; the extra action rides along uninflected.

That is why they matter more than their size suggests. Until this chapter a Sanskrit sentence in this book had exactly one action in it, unless two clauses were pinned together with a pronoun pair or with \textbf{\sk{इति}}. From here a single clause can carry two.

Keep the contrast, because it is the only thing you have to choose between:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{-\sk{त्वा}} — the action \textbf{happened first}
  \item \textbf{-\sk{तुम्}} — the action is \textbf{the point of the other one}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ gṛhaṁ gatvā paṭhati}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ paṭhitum gacchati}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} say which sentence has the reading happen first
  \item \emph{Recall:} the Latin ending that matches \textbf{-\sk{तुम्}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say both endings and, for each, one sentence that uses it.
\end{tcolorbox}
